name: Bootes
introduction: is the Herdsman, usually pictured driving the bears around the pole. Its stars form a kite shape, with brilliant orange Arcturus at its tail. To find it, follow the curve of the Big Dipper’s handle: “arc to Arcturus”. It is best seen on northern spring and summer evenings.

sections.title: What makes it special
paragraphs: [Arcturus](hip:69673), 37 light-years away, is the brightest star in the northern half of the sky and the fourth-brightest in the night sky. It is an old orange giant, about 25 times wider than the Sun, moving through our part of the galaxy much faster than most stars. In 1933, light from Arcturus was used to switch on the lights at the Chicago World’s Fair.
Arcturus and [Muphrid](hip:67927) are both about 37 light-years away, and only about three light-years from each other. Seen from one, the other would be a brilliant star in its sky.

sections.title: Notable stars
paragraphs: [Izar](hip:72105), also called Pulcherrima, “the most beautiful”, is a stunning double star in a telescope: a golden giant with a small blue-green companion.

[Seginus](hip:71075) and [Nekkar](hip:73555) mark the herdsman’s shoulders and head. The faint star Tau Boötis, nearby, was one of the first stars found to host a hot Jupiter, a giant planet orbiting very close to its star.

sections.title: Beyond the stars
paragraphs: Early each January, the Quadrantid meteor shower radiates from northern Boötes. It is named after the old, now-retired constellation Quadrans Muralis. Far beyond the stars lies the Boötes Void, an almost empty region of space about 330 million light-years across, with very few galaxies.
